ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Mark Twain Synthetic CCD

text.paragraph: Establishing primary care a year after his wife's death: yearning, poor sleep, low mood and withdrawal, suicide risk, heavy cigar smoking, chest tightness on hills, gout and cardiovascular risk. Concerns: He says the year since his wife died has not softened anything, and he wants to be able to work and see his friends again; He does not want to give up cigars, which he says help him write, but worries about his heart; He wants the gout attacks to stop. [S]

list.item: Writer, humorist and lecturer for more than forty years; known by his pen name; writing most mornings but unable to finish anything since his wife died [S]

Widowed a year ago after 34 years of marriage; has lost a son in early childhood and a daughter as a young woman; lives in a rented house in the hills for the summer with a family member, a secretary and household staff; no relative is named or given a role in this record [S]

Tobacco: cigars since boyhood, now about fifteen a day and a pipe in the evening, with some smoke inhaled; has stopped for months at a time before and always started again; says cigars help him write [S]
Alcohol: a glass of whisky most evenings (AUDIT-C 3); no other drugs [S]
Finances: lost everything in a business failure about ten years ago and repaid his creditors by lecturing; secure now; still anxious about money at night [S]
No firearms in the house; walks the hill roads most days [S]
Strengths: humor, a lifetime of writing, many friends and admirers, neighbors in the summer colony who visit, a daily routine of work, and his own decision to come in [S]

tr.td: Establishing primary care a year after his wife's death: yearning, poor sleep, low mood and withdrawal, suicide risk, heavy cigar smoking, chest tightness on hills, gout and cardiovascular risk
One-week review, seen the same day by geriatric psychiatry: the diagnosis of prolonged grief disorder, grief therapy, sleep and safety
Five-week review: CT coronary angiography result, a statin and aspirin, a plan to quit smoking, and starting allopurinol
Thirteen-week review: grief therapy, smoking, a gout flare while away, the urate and lipid results
Eighteen-week review: grief, no smoking, urate toward target and his writing
Same-day sick visit for a cough
Geriatric psychiatry consultation to confirm the diagnosis, separate prolonged grief disorder from major depression, advise on grief therapy, medicine and sleep, and review suicide risk
Safety: a structured safety assessment, a written safety plan, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in his phone, means safety, a telephone call in three days, and safety review at every visit

Prolonged grief disorder therapy (Shear): sixteen weekly sessions with a trained psychologist, covering the story of the death, imaginal conversations with his wife, memories and pictures, revisiting avoided places and things, and personal goals; PG-13-R and PHQ-9 every four weeks; no antidepressant unless major depression develops

Sleep: a fixed rising time, no naps after noon, no cigar or whisky in the last hours before bed, and getting up if awake more than twenty minutes; no benzodiazepine, zolpidem or sedating antihistamine

Tobacco: his readiness asked at every visit; brief advice linked to his own concern about his heart; counseling at each visit and the state quitline; varenicline offered as the most effective single medicine, with combination nicotine replacement as the alternative

Chest tightness on exertion: resting ECG today and CT coronary angiography, chosen over stress testing for a man over 65 with stable symptoms and no known coronary disease; call 911 for chest pain at rest or lasting more than fifteen minutes

Nonobstructive coronary disease: atorvastatin 40 mg with a lipid panel 4 to 12 weeks later and a goal of at least a 50 percent fall in LDL, aspirin 81 mg, blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg, stopping smoking, and walking most days

Gout: allopurinol from 100 mg daily, raised by 100 mg every two to five weeks to a serum urate below 6 mg/dL, with colchicine 0.6 mg daily for three to six months to prevent flares; flares treated without stopping allopurinol; HLA-B*58:01 testing not indicated by ancestry; less alcohol

Social connection and his writing: one planned social contact a week, a return to morning writing on a set project, and the clinic social worker's list of local groups; meaning and goals to be part of any grief treatment

Gout: urate measured at intake; urate-lowering therapy explained, since two flares in a year make it strongly recommended; he chose to decide after the chest evaluation; call at the first sign of a flare
Cardiovascular risk: blood pressure at each visit and lipids, hemoglobin A1c and kidney function at baseline; prediabetes (hemoglobin A1c 5.8 percent) managed with walking and diet
PG-13-R below 30 and back to writing and seeing friends
PG-13-R 41 at intake to 26 at eighteen weeks; finishing a long essay; dinner with friends weekly
No thoughts of death and a safety plan he would use
Passive thoughts of death at intake; none since the five-week visit; safety plan kept
Fifteen cigars a day at intake; quit in the first week of August with varenicline; one lapse of two cigars while away; none for eight weeks
LDL cholesterol at least 50 percent lower on a high-intensity statin
LDL 150 to 74 mg/dL (51 percent lower) at eight weeks
Serum urate below 6 mg/dL and no gout flares
Urate 8.6, 7.4 and 6.4 mg/dL; one flare in August, treated while away; allopurinol raised to 300 mg
Six or more hours of sleep on most nights without a sleeping pill
About four to five hours at intake; six hours on most nights by eighteen weeks

list.item: Independent in all activities and instrumental activities; has stopped seeing friends and turned down every invitation since the winter [S]

Alert and oriented; courteous, dryly funny even while tearful; speech normal; mood "hollow"; talks of his wife in the present tense and keeps her room as it was; yearning and preoccupation every day; some days wishes he could join her, without any intent or plan; no hallucinations apart from sometimes hearing her voice as he falls asleep, which he knows is not real; thinking clear [S]

text.paragraph: Structured synthetic safety assessment on 2026-06-12: current ideation present, intent absent, plan absent. Outpatient care with weekly visits and a telephone call in three days. Passive thoughts of death (wishing he could join his wife) without intent, plan or preparation; no past suicide attempt. Older widowed men are at high risk of suicide in the years after a loss (a Danish register study found the highest rise in suicide risk in the oldest bereaved men), and he has several further risk factors: repeated bereavement, living through the anniversary of her death, insomnia, alcohol each evening, chronic illness and social withdrawal. Means safety: no firearms in the house; medicines kept in small supplies; he agreed to keep whisky to one glass and none on bad nights. A written safety plan was made with him, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) was saved in his phone. Safety is reviewed at every visit [S]
